stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pallor, and difficulty swallowing solids. She also reports a history of heavy menstrual bleeding. On examination, conjunctival pallor is noted. Laboratory investigations reveal:
Hemoglobin: 8.5 g/dL
MCV: 70 fL
RDW: increased
Ferritin: 5 ng/mL
Which of the following is the most likely cause of her anemia? (Question Id: 501016)
stemHtml:
A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pallor, and difficulty swallowing solids. She also reports a history of heavy menstrual bleeding. On examination, conjunctival pallor is noted. Laboratory investigations reveal:

  • Hemoglobin: 8.5 g/dL
  • MCV: 70 fL
  • RDW: increased
  • Ferritin: 5 ng/mL

Which of the following is the most likely cause of her anemia? (Question Id: 501016)
keywords: Heavy menstrual bleeding → Indicates chronic blood loss, the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in reproductive-age women.
Ferritin 5 ng/mL → Definitive marker of depleted iron stores; the most specific lab for iron deficiency.
Dysphagia for solids → Suggests Plummer–Vinson syndrome, strongly linked with long-standing iron deficiency.
keywordsHtml:
1. Heavy menstrual bleeding → Indicates chronic blood loss, the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in reproductive-age women.
  2. Ferritin 5 ng/mL → Definitive marker of depleted iron stores; the most specific lab for iron deficiency.
  3. Dysphagia for solids → Suggests Plummer–Vinson syndrome, strongly linked with long-standing iron deficiency.

A.title: Iron deficiency anemia
A.body:
The patient has classic symptoms (fatigue, pallor) plus dysphagia for solids, suggesting Plummer–Vinson syndrome, which is strongly associated with chronic iron deficiency.
Lab Findings:
Hemoglobin (8.5 g/dL): Confirms anemia.
MCV (70 fL): Indicates microcytic anemia (low mean corpuscular volume, <80 fL).
RDW (Increased): Suggests significant anisocytosis (variation in red blood cell size), which is very common in IDA due to the bone marrow attempting to produce new cells under iron-deficient conditions.
Ferritin (5 ng/mL): Ferritin is the body's main iron storage protein. A very low ferritin level (<10-15 ng/mL) is the single most reliable test for diagnosing true iron deficiency.
The combination of microcytic anemia and markedly low ferritin confirms the diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia.
The clinical clue of heavy menstrual bleeding identifies the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in reproductive-age women.
A.bodyHtml:
• The patient has classic symptoms (fatigue, pallor) plus dysphagia for solids, suggesting Plummer–Vinson syndrome, which is strongly associated with chronic iron deficiency.
  • Lab Findings:
    • Hemoglobin (8.5 g/dL): Confirms anemia.
    • MCV (70 fL): Indicates microcytic anemia (low mean corpuscular volume, <80 fL).
    • RDW (Increased): Suggests significant anisocytosis (variation in red blood cell size), which is very common in IDA due to the bone marrow attempting to produce new cells under iron-deficient conditions.
    • Ferritin (5 ng/mL): Ferritin is the body's main iron storage protein. A very low ferritin level (<10-15 ng/mL) is the single most reliable test for diagnosing true iron deficiency.
  • The combination of microcytic anemia and markedly low ferritin confirms the diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia.
  • The clinical clue of heavy menstrual bleeding identifies the most common cause of iron deficiency anemia in reproductive-age women.

B.title: Anemia of chronic disease
B.body:
Usually presents with normal or high ferritin because it is an acute-phase reactant.
MCV is often normal or mildly decreased, and RDW is typically normal, unlike this patient.
B.bodyHtml:
• Usually presents with normal or high ferritin because it is an acute-phase reactant.
  • MCV is often normal or mildly decreased, and RDW is typically normal, unlike this patient.

C.title: Beta-thalassemia minor
C.body:
Shows very low MCV but normal RDW and normal or raised RBC count.
Ferritin is usually normal. Does not cause dysphagia or heavy bleeding.
C.bodyHtml:
• Shows very low MCV but normal RDW and normal or raised RBC count.
  • Ferritin is usually normal. Does not cause dysphagia or heavy bleeding.

D.title: Sideroblastic anemia
D.body:
Characterized by high iron levels and high ferritin, not low ferritin.
Bone marrow shows ring sideroblasts, and it does not present with Plummer–Vinson features.
D.bodyHtml:
• Characterized by high iron levels and high ferritin, not low ferritin.
  • Bone marrow shows ring sideroblasts, and it does not present with Plummer–Vinson features.

E.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency
E.body:
Causes macrocytic anemia (MCV >100 fL), not microcytic.
Neurological symptoms may occur; ferritin is normal or increased.
E.bodyHtml:
• Causes macrocytic anemia (MCV >100 fL), not microcytic.
  • Neurological symptoms may occur; ferritin is normal or increased.

keyConcept: Iron deficiency anemia presents with microcytic anemia, high RDW, and low ferritin, commonly due to chronic blood loss in women. Dysphagia in this context suggests Plummer–Vinson syndrome, a classic association with long-standing iron deficiency.

tables.heading: Microcytic Anemia – Iron Deficiency Anemia (Clinical Hematology)

cells: Definition

Microcytic,
hypochromic anemia due to depleted iron stores
Most common anemia worldwide, especially in women
cellsHtml:
• Microcytic,
  • hypochromic anemia due to depleted iron stores
Most common anemia worldwide, especially in women

cells: Causes

Chronic blood loss (menorrhagia, GI bleed),
low dietary intake,
increased demand
Identifying cause is essential for long-term correction
cellsHtml:
• Chronic blood loss (menorrhagia, GI bleed),
  • low dietary intake,
  • increased demand
Identifying cause is essential for long-term correction

cells: Lab Findings

↓ Ferritin,
↑ TIBC,
↓ Serum iron,
↑ RDW,
MCV < 80 fL
Confirms iron deficiency and differentiates from other microcytic anemias
cellsHtml:
• ↓ Ferritin,
  • ↑ TIBC,
  • ↓ Serum iron,
  • ↑ RDW,
  • MCV < 80 fL
Confirms iron deficiency and differentiates from other microcytic anemias

cells: Clinical Features

Fatigue,
pallor,
pica,
koilonychia,
glossitis;
may include dysphagia (Plummer–Vinson)
Helps clinch diagnosis before labs
Management
Response seen as ↑ reticulocytes within 7–10 days
cellsHtml:
• Treat cause;
  • oral iron therapy (ferrous sulfate);
  • IV iron if malabsorption

Normal or ↑ Ferritin,
↓ TIBC,
mild microcytosis

Thalassemia Minor (α or β)

ferritin normal

• Very low MCV,

High iron,
↑ ferritin,

ring sideroblasts in marrow

not low

• High iron,

cells: Lead Poisoning

Basophilic stippling,
abdominal pain,
neuropathy;
normal/↑ ferritin
Toxic exposure + stippling → not seen in IDA
cellsHtml: Toxic exposure + stippling → not seen in IDA

diagrams.heading: Microcytic Anemia – Iron Deficiency Anemia (Clinical Overview Diagram)
diagrams.headingHtml:
Microcytic Anemia – Iron Deficiency Anemia

(Clinical Overview Diagram)
diagrams.description: This diagram illustrates the pathophysiology, causes, clinical features, laboratory findings, and management of iron deficiency anemia. It highlights microcytic, hypochromic red blood cells with key lab markers such as low MCV and low ferritin, along with common causes like chronic blood loss and poor dietary intake. Clinical manifestations (fatigue, pica, koilonychia) and treatment strategies (oral and IV iron therapy) are also visually summarized for quick understanding.
